prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute widespread active denervation on EMG to anxiety or deconditioning — this represents clinically manifest motor neuron disease requiring urgent diagnostic and prognostic workup.
Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine): no benefit in bvFTD-MND and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.

Do not dismiss mildly elevated CK as a primary myopathy or as diagnostic of inflammatory myositis — in this context, mild CK elevation is a non-specific finding consistent with neurogenic muscle denervation; muscle biopsy is not indicated without additional features of primary myopathy.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition, respiratory depression (particularly hazardous given declining FVC), and falls.
required_recommendations: Perform EMG/NCS to confirm motor neuron disease — clinical motor signs (Babinski, fasciculations, weakness, brisk reflexes) in a behavioral dementia patient mandate electrodiagnostic evaluation to establish FTD-MND.
Monitor respiratory function (FVC upright and supine, MIP, MEP) at 3-month intervals; FVC below 50% predicted triggers non-invasive ventilation discussion.
Order C9orf72 genetic testing given father died of ALS and paternal aunt had behavioral dementia — autosomal dominant inheritance pattern is highly suggestive.
Provide genetic counseling and offer cascade testing to first-degree relatives (brother, adult children) given confirmed C9orf72 expansion.

Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (patient meets ≥5 of 6 core features: disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseveration/stereotypy, hyperorality/dietary changes, executive dysfunction) and document functional decline.
Assess driving safety, financial decision-making capacity, and occupational safety given progression of executive dysfunction and motor impairment.

Do not attribute EMG-confirmed denervation in four regions to anxiety or benign fasciculation syndrome; benign fasciculation syndrome does not cause active denervation, reinnervation, or upper motor neuron signs.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggests CJD or autoimmune encephalitis — neither present here.
ECG has no role in the cognitive or neuromuscular workup of FTD-MND; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD-MND and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity to characterize frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; no parkinsonism or concern for PD/DLB/PSP is present — it is not indicated in FTD-MND.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD-MND diagnostic pathway.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia with motor neuron disease (FTD-MND)

differential.key_features: Upper and lower motor neuron signs present, but behavioral syndrome (apathy, disinhibition, loss of empathy, perseveration) and frontotemporal atrophy precede motor symptoms and are prominent — exceeds what could be attributed to ALS-associated cognitive changes.
Behavioral change is prominent and memory relatively preserved; hippocampal volume normal; posterior cortex spared — pattern atypical for AD. Motor neuron signs absent in AD.

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (major depressive disorder with psychomotor features or late-onset personality disorder)
differential.key_features: Failed two antidepressant trials; progressive informant-reported functional decline; objective executive deficits on testing; motor signs not explained by psychiatric diagnosis.

differential.diagnosis: Progressive supranuclear palsy with behavioral variant FTD phenotype (PSP-bvFTD)
differential.key_features: No supranuclear gaze palsy, no early falls, no axial rigidity, no midbrain atrophy — PSP features absent. Lower motor neuron signs on EMG favor FTD-MND over PSP.

EMG shows active denervation and reinnervation in four regions, far exceeding what is expected in benign fasciculation syndrome (which is EMG-normal except for fasciculation potentials alone). Upper motor neuron signs (Babinski, brisk reflexes, Hoffman) also exclude this diagnosis.

key_clinical_evidence: The behavioral syndrome (apathy, disinhibition, loss of empathy, perseveration, hyperorality, executive dysfunction — meeting ≥5 Rascovsky 2011 criteria) defines bvFTD; the co-occurring upper and lower motor neuron signs (Babinski, brisk reflexes, Hoffman, tongue and limb fasciculations, tibialis anterior weakness) define FTD-MND — these are two parallel diagnostic streams that must be synthesized, not treated as competing diagnoses.

Motor signs (fasciculations, cramps, foot drag, subtle weakness) were present 14 months before this evaluation but were dismissed as anxiety and deconditioning — the anchor on anxiety history is the primary diagnostic trap; the puzzle is solved only by recognizing that anxiety does not produce active EMG denervation in four regions, Babinski signs, or brisk jaw jerk.

The family history (father with ALS, paternal aunt with dementia) is a strong signal for C9orf72 autosomal dominant disease — the same expansion can cause pure ALS, pure FTD, or combined FTD-MND in different family members, which is the hallmark of C9orf72 spectrum disease.

FVC 72% upright and 63% supine with a 13-percentage-point postural drop indicates early diaphragm weakness; this changes prognosis and requires serial monitoring — at FVC 50% predicted, NIV discussions begin, making respiratory function testing a load-bearing required step in FTD-MND.

Mildly elevated CK (318 U/L, 1.7x ULN) in the context of widespread denervation is a non-specific neurogenic finding — it must not anchor a myopathy workup or distract from the combined upper and lower motor neuron phenotype.

FDG-PET adds premotor/motor cortex hypometabolism to the frontotemporal pattern, consistent with the motor system involvement; this metabolic signature in bvFTD should prompt re-evaluation for FTD-MND even when the initial referral framing was purely cognitive.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Generalized anxiety disorder does not cause tongue fasciculations, bilateral Babinski signs, brisk jaw jerk, Hoffman's sign, or active EMG denervation in four regions; the motor signs require electrodiagnostic evaluation independent of the anxiety history.

results.finding: C9orf72 GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat expansion is the most common known genetic cause of familial motor neuron disease and familial frontal-network neurodegeneration, with a single mutation accounting for both phenotypes within and across families.
results.title: A hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9ORF72 underlies chromosome 9p21-linked motor neuron disease and frontal-network neurodegeneration

results.finding: FTD-MND overlap occurs in 10-15% of FTD cases; behavioral features of bvFTD may precede, coincide with, or follow motor neuron disease onset; prognosis is significantly shorter than pure FTD (median survival 2-3 years from motor onset). C9orf72 is the most common identified genetic cause.
results.title: Frontotemporal dementia. Bang J et al. Lancet 2015;386:1672-1682.

results.finding: C9orf72 repeat expansion accounts for approximately 25-40% of familial FTD and 40% of familial ALS; same expansion can cause pure FTD, pure ALS, or FTD-ALS phenotype. Genetic testing is indicated in patients with young-onset FTD or a family history of ALS or FTD. Autosomal dominant inheritance with high but incomplete penetrance.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. V. is a 56-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman, a bilingual education coordinator, who presents to the cognitive neurology clinic accompanied by her husband. Her husband is the primary historian, as Ms. V. minimizes her difficulties and attributes them to stress and aging. Over the past 18 months, her husband has observed a profound personality transformation in a woman he describes as formerly warm, organized, and professionally accomplished. She has developed striking apathy — she stopped gardening (a lifelong passion), quit cooking family meals, and spends 6-8 hours per day passively watching television without responding to its content. She has become disinhibited: she laughed audibly at a family funeral, comments openly on strangers' physical appearance in public, and has made off-color remarks that are entirely out of character. She has lost empathy — when her husband was hospitalized briefly for a cardiac procedure 6 months ago, she showed no concern and did not call to check on him during the procedure. She repeats the same three anecdotes in nearly every conversation and has developed a rigid food preference for sweets. She does not recognize that her behavior has changed and actively resists the idea that she needs evaluation.

Beyond the cognitive-behavioral changes, her husband notes she has been complaining of muscle twitching, cramps, and fatigue for 14 months. She stopped her daily 3-mile walks citing leg fatigue and cramps. Her speech has become subtly slurred, which she attributes to 'talking too fast.' She has had no falls but her husband has noticed she drags her left foot occasionally. These motor symptoms were evaluated by her primary care physician 9 months ago; he attributed them to anxiety, deconditioning, and possibly benign fasciculation syndrome given her anxiety history. He ordered routine labs and recommended therapy and magnesium supplementation.

Family history is highly significant: her father died of ALS at age 58. Her paternal aunt developed behavioral changes in her early 60s and was diagnosed with dementia, dying in memory care. The patient is unaware of any genetic link between ALS and dementia. Her psychiatrist referred her to this clinic after noting that her apathy and personality change were not responsive to two trials of antidepressants and were progressing.

neurological_exam.additional: Husband reports progressive behavioral change over 18 months: increased apathy (quit gardening, stopped cooking family meals, watching TV for 6-8 hours per day), disinhibition (laughed at a funeral, made loud personal comments about a neighbor's appearance), and loss of empathy (unresponsive to husband's distress during significant family illness). She eats the same two meals on rotation and has developed a preference for very sweet foods (candy, pastries). She has been forgetting recent conversations but remembers remote events in detail. Prior evaluation by her primary care physician 9 months ago attributed fasciculations and muscle cramps to anxiety, deconditioning, and possible benign fasciculation syndrome. She was referred back to therapy and started on magnesium supplements.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements full with no nystagmus. Facial sensation symmetric. Facial activation symmetric. Tongue protrudes in midline — fine tongue fasciculations visible at rest, two to three beats per minute. Palate elevation symmetric. Gag intact bilaterally. Mild slurring of rapid syllable repetition ('pa-ta-ka') — patient attributes to 'talking fast.' Jaw jerk mildly brisk.
neurological_exam.gait: Slightly wide-based, mildly spastic quality — drags left foot intermittently. No cerebellar ataxia. Tandem gait mildly impaired (2 steps off-line). Unable to perform tandem walking for 10 steps.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x3. Affect notably flat; makes two jokes at socially inappropriate moments during exam and shows no embarrassment when corrected. MoCA 23/30: loses 3 points on executive tasks (alternating trails, verbal fluency — 6 F-words in 1 minute; 10 animals in 1 minute, borderline), 2 on delayed recall (recalls 1/5 at 5 minutes, recognizes 4/5 with cues — suggests mild retrieval deficit rather than storage failure), 1 on abstraction. Husband reports she has been making repetitive comments and asking the same questions repeatedly for the past year.

neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 3+ bilaterally. Plantar responses: extensor (Babinski) bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in all four limbs.
